Ur III was a kingdom ruled from the city of Ur in southern Mesopotamia from about 2112 to 2004 BCE, the last great state of the Sumerians. Historians also call it the Neo-Sumerian Empire. It is named as the third dynasty of Ur in the old Mesopotamian king lists.

Its founder, Ur-Nammu, took power after the fall of the Akkadian Empire. He built the Ziggurat of Ur and issued the Code of Ur-Nammu, the oldest law code that survives.

His son Shulgi ruled for about 48 years and built one of the most organised states of the ancient world:

  • He set standard weights, measures and a state calendar.
  • Provinces paid taxes in turn into a central system of goods and animals.
  • Scribes recorded almost everything. Tens of thousands of their clay tablets survive, listing workers, rations, sheep and beer.

Sumerian writing flourished, and many of the Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh may come from this court, the earliest pieces of the Epic of Gilgamesh.

The state was strong but short-lived. Semitic-speaking Amorites moved in from the west, and the kings built a long wall to keep them out. Provinces broke away. In 2004 BCE an army from Elam sacked Ur and carried off its last king, Ibbi-Sin. Scribes mourned it in the Lament for Ur. After Ur III, Amorite kings ruled the region, and power moved north to cities like Babylon and the Old Babylonian kingdom.
